analysis.investment_thesis: MedPlus fails both Magic Formula tests: Earnings Yield of ~4.2% (EBIT INR 488 Cr / EV ~INR 11,578 Cr) is well below my 6% minimum, and ROCE of 10.3% is far short of the 20%+ threshold I demand for a quality business. At 51x P/E and 28x EV/EBITDA for a thin-margin pharmacy retailer, I'm being asked to pay a premium price for a mediocre business.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 15.1% over 9 years with operating income growing faster (33.2% CAGR) — clear operating leverage emerging.
FCF surged to INR 482 Cr in FY2025 after years of near-zero or negative free cash, suggesting the store rollout phase is maturing.
Institutional confidence: DII + FII combined ownership of ~43% signals professional validation of the long-run pharmacy consolidation story.
key_risks: Earnings Yield of ~4.2% is deeply unattractive — I need at least 6%, ideally 12%+; the stock is priced for perfection it hasn't yet demonstrated.
Operating margins of 4.75% leave almost no buffer — finance costs of INR 103 Cr consumed 69% of FY2025 net profit of INR 150 Cr.
Earnings volatility is alarming: net profit went INR 2 Cr → 63 → 95 → 50 → 66 → 150 Cr over six years; this is not the consistent earnings power I need.
red_flags: ROCE of 10.3% and ROE of 8.8% — both well below cost of capital for a levered retailer; the business is not earning adequate returns on deployed capital.
Total debt grew from INR 815 Cr (FY2022) to INR 1,193 Cr (FY2025) while equity base grew partly via IPO proceeds — organic capital generation is weak.
EV/EBITDA of 28x for a sub-5% operating margin retailer is difficult to justify under any conservative earnings growth scenario.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running MedPlus through the Magic Formula is straightforward and swift. Earnings Yield: EBIT of INR 488 Cr divided by Enterprise Value of ~INR 11,578 Cr (market cap INR 10,544 Cr + debt INR 1,120 Cr − cash INR 86 Cr) = 4.2%. That's well below my 6% floor, let alone the 12–15% zone where I get excited. Return on Capital: ROCE as reported is 10.3%, and even using invested capital (equity + debt − cash ≈ INR 2,879 Cr), EBIT/IC is roughly 17% — better, but largely inflated by IND-AS 116 lease capitalization that simultaneously pumps EBITDA and debt. The true cash-on-cash economics of running a pharmacy store network are much thinner than headline numbers suggest.

The business story is understandable — India's pharmacy retail is fragmented and MedPlus is one of the few scaled organized players — but being in a good industry doesn't make a stock a good investment. At 51x trailing earnings, the market is pricing in sustained double-digit profit growth that the company's own history doesn't support (net profit has been volatile and sub-scale relative to revenue for a decade). Free cash flow turned meaningfully positive in FY2025 (INR 482 Cr), which is encouraging, but one year of strong FCF after years of near-zero conversion is not the sustained, compounding capital efficiency that the Magic Formula demands. I'll pass and look elsewhere.
